source_text: Processerit, age, iam in notitiam quando uoluit, quando potuit, quando hora fatalis aduenit. fortasse enim anabibazon ei obstabat aut aliquae maleficae aut Saturnus quadratus aut Mars trigonus. nam et mathematici plurimum Marcionitae, nec hoc erubescentes, de ipsis etiam stellis uiuere creatoris. tractandum est hic de reuelationis qualitate, an digne reuelatus sit, ut constet, an uere, et ita credatur esse quem digne constiterit reuelatum. digna enim deo probabunt deum. nos definimus deum primo natura cognoscendum, dehinc doctrina recognoscendum, natura ex operibus, doctrina ex praedicationibus. sed cui nulla natura est naturalia instrumenta non suppetunt. ergo uel praedicationibus reuelationem sui debuerat operari, maxime aduersus eum reuelandus, qui et conditionis et praedicationis operibus tot ac tantis uix tamen hominem fide impleuerat. quomodo itaque cognitus est? si per humanam coniecturam, nego deum alias cognosci posse quam per semetipsum, nec tantum ad formam prouocans creatoris uerum et ad condicionem tam diuinae magnitudinis quam humanae mediocritatis, ne maior deo homo uideri possit, qui eum non ultro uolentem cognosci suis uiribus quodammodo in publicum agnitionis extraxerit, cum humana mediocritas facilius deos fingere sibi norit secundum totius aeui experimenta quam uerum sectari, quem natura iam intellegunt. alioquin, si sic homo d.-\'um commentabitur, quomodo Romulus Consum et Tatius Cloacinam et Hostilius Pauorem et Metellus Alburnum et quidam ante hoc tempus Antinoum, hoc aliis licebit; nos Marciouem nauclerum nouimus, non regem nec imperatorem.
pass_a_gloss: Let him proceed, now, into recognition when he wished, when he was able, when the fatal hour arrived. For perhaps the ascending node was obstructing him or some evil influences or Saturn square or Mars in trine. For even the mathematicians, many of whom are Marcionites, and they are not ashamed of this, live from the very stars of the creator. The quality of the revelation must be treated here, whether he was revealed worthily, so that it may be consistent, whether truly, and thus it may be believed to be what has been revealed worthily. For things worthy of God will prove God. We define God as first to be known by nature, then to be recognized by doctrine, by nature from works, by doctrine from preachings. But to whom no nature is, natural instruments are not sufficient. Therefore, either he ought to have operated the revelation of himself by preachings, especially to be revealed against him who, by the works of condition and preaching, had barely filled man with faith, and that with so many and such great works. How, therefore, was he known? If by human conjecture, I deny that God can be known otherwise than by himself, and not only to the form of the creator, but also to the condition of such divine greatness and human mediocrity, lest man may seem greater than God, who has not willingly been known, and has been led into public recognition by his own powers, when human mediocrity knows how to fashion gods for itself more easily, according to the experiments of all time, than to follow the truth, which nature already understands. Otherwise, if man thus comments on God, how Romulus worshipped Consus and Tatius Cloacina and Hostilius Pavor and Metellus Alburnus, and some before this time Antinous, this will be allowed to others; we know Marcion as a shipowner, not as a king or emperor.

choices.why: refers to the act of revealing

pass_b_english: Let him proceed, then, into recognition — when he wished, when he could, when the fatal hour arrived. Perhaps the ascending node blocked him, or some baleful influence, or Saturn in square, or Mars in trine. After all, the mathematicians are mostly Marcionites, and they don't blush to admit it; they live by the very stars of the Creator.

Here we must test the quality of the revelation: whether he was revealed worthily, so that it holds together; whether truly, so that he may be believed to be what he was worthily revealed to be. Things worthy of God will prove God.

We define God as first to be known by nature, then recognized by doctrine — nature from his works, doctrine from his preachings. But where there is no nature, natural instruments fail. So he ought to have effected his own revelation through preachings, especially against the one who needed revealing — the one who, despite works of creation and preaching so many and so great, had barely managed to fill man with faith.

How, then, was he known? If by human conjecture, I deny that God can be known except by himself — and not merely to the form of the Creator, but to the condition of such divine greatness and human mediocrity, lest man appear greater than God. God did not will to be known; he was dragged into public recognition by his own powers. Human mediocrity finds it easier to fabricate gods for itself, based on the experiments of all time, than to follow the truth that nature already grasps.

Otherwise, if man presumes to comment on God this way, then let others do as Romulus did with Consus, Tatius with Cloacina, Hostilius with Pavor, Metellus with Alburnus, and some before this time with Antinous. We know Marcion as a shipowner, not a king or emperor.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text, including the astrological terms (anabibazon, Saturnus quadratus, Mars trigonus) and the list of mythological/historical figures. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the source. The distinction between 'natura' and 'doctrina' is preserved. The translation of 'conditionis' as 'creation' in Pass B is a slight interpretive shift from 'condition' in Pass A, but in the context of Marcionite theology (works of creation vs works of preaching), it remains faithful to the sense of the argument.

The Latin text is correctly identified as 'Against Marcion 1.18' from the specified source. The English translation accurately reflects the content of the Latin, preserving the meaning, structure, and key terms. All citations and references are consistent with the source material.
